title: Concurrent collections and Channels (message passing)
hook: ConcurrentDictionary and ConcurrentQueue let many threads add and remove without wrapping Dictionary in lock. System.Threading.Channels provide producer-consumer queues with async read and write — a cleaner model than sharing a locked list between RabbitMQ handlers.

blocks.text: Concurrent collections in System.Collections.Concurrent use fine-grained locking or lock-free techniques for thread-safe operations. ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue> supports TryAdd and GetOrAdd atomically. Channel<T> is a bounded or unbounded queue: writers call WriteAsync; readers use await foreach or ReadAsync. Multiple consumers can compete for items safely.

entries.plainDefinition: Thread-safe dictionary with atomic add/update operations.
Async producer-consumer queue for passing messages between threads.
Producers enqueue work; consumers dequeue and process independently.
entries.example: RabbitMQ receiver writes to channel; worker tasks read from channel.

blocks.text: Hand-rolled lock + List<T> for a work queue serializes every enqueue and dequeue. Channels decouple receive thread from processing threads and support backpressure with bounded capacity. ConcurrentDictionary is the right tool for a shared cache map — not Dictionary with lock on every read unless profiling shows you need finer control.

blocks.title: When not to invent
blocks.body: Use BCL concurrent types before building your own lock-free queue. Module 08 covers when custom structures are justified.

items.body: Capacity limits memory when producers outpace consumers.

items.title: Producer writes
items.body: RabbitMQ handler awaits WriteAsync — does not process inline.

items.body: Multiple readers await ReadAsync in parallel.

items.title: Complete channel
items.body: Writer.Complete() signals no more items; readers drain and finish.

snippet.label: ConcurrentDictionary cache
snippet.explanation: GetOrAdd ensures only one factory runs per key even under concurrent requests.

snippet.label: Bounded channel setup
snippet.explanation: When 500 items are buffered, WriteAsync waits — backpressure instead of unbounded memory growth.

snippet.label: Consumer loop
snippet.explanation: ReadAllAsync yields messages as they arrive. Multiple consumers can each run this loop on the same reader.

snippet.label: Multiple channel consumers
snippet.explanation: Four parallel consumers compete fairly for channel items — scales processing without locking a shared List.

Async queue libraries or EventEmitter patterns

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Unbounded channel when producers can flood memory. Assuming ConcurrentDictionary values are immutable — mutate copies or use locks inside values. Forgetting Writer.Complete() so readers hang forever.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: ConcurrentDictionary uses striped locks — high write contention on one bucket still serializes. Channels decouple producers from consumers with optional backpressure; monitor channel depth via custom metrics or log when WriteAsync blocks. For RabbitMQ ingestion, a bounded Channel between receive and workers prevents memory blow-up when ProcessAsync slows. dotnet-counters won't show channel depth directly — instrument Count or time spent in WriteAsync.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Per-bucket locking; GetOrAdd atomic per key
Avoid — Channels or concurrent collections win

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Treating ConcurrentDictionary as making mutable values thread-safe — two threads mutating the same UserDto still races. Unbounded Channel in a burst SQS consumer — OOM under spike. Using ConcurrentQueue when you need async backpressure — callers spin or block manually. Single consumer on a Channel when CPU-bound processing could parallelize.

interviewTakeaways: ConcurrentDictionary provides thread-safe map operations; Channel provides async producer-consumer queues with optional bounded backpressure.
Values inside ConcurrentDictionary are not magically immutable — coordinate mutations inside the value or store immutable snapshots.
In production, bound Channels between fast ingress (RabbitMQ/SQS) and slow workers; alert when WriteAsync wait time grows.

60s: ConcurrentDictionary for shared maps and single-flight. Channel for async pipelines with backpressure. Multiple ReadAllAsync consumers for parallel processing. Never unbounded under burst traffic.
Follow-up: when is message passing (Channel) strictly better than a concurrent map?
commonPitfalls: Saying ConcurrentDictionary makes object graphs thread-safe gets you rejected — only dictionary operations are coordinated.
Unbounded channel in burst traffic — memory grows until OOM.
Strong answer: 'Channel for pipeline decoupling with bounded capacity. ConcurrentDictionary for keyed caches. Immutable values or internal locks on mutable DTOs.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: p-queue and similar npm packages mirror bounded worker queues. C# Channels are built into the runtime.
await for...of on async iterables resembles ReadAllAsync — both pull items sequentially, but C# Channels support multiple competing consumers safely.
